title: Electrolit vs Gatorade: Which Is Better for Hangovers?
excerpt: Electrolit vs Gatorade compared: sodium, sugar, and what each is built for, which works better for a hangover, stomach bug, or workout, how Gatorlyte and Gatorade Zero fit in, and honest pros and cons.
metaDescription: Electrolit vs Gatorade: sodium, sugar, and which is better for a hangover, stomach bug, or workout, plus how Gatorlyte and Gatorade Zero compare.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Electrolit and Gatorade look like they sit on the same shelf, but they're built for different jobs. Electrolit is an oral rehydration drink, the kind of *suero* people in Mexico keep in the fridge for stomach bugs, heat, and *la cruda*. Regular Gatorade is a sports drink designed to fuel athletes who are sweating for hours. For a hangover, a stomach bug, or any time you've actually lost fluid from vomiting or diarrhea, Electrolit is usually the better choice: it carries more sodium and less sugar, which is the mix your gut needs to pull water back in. For a long, hard workout, regular Gatorade's extra sugar is a feature, not a bug. And if your store only has Gatorade products, **Gatorlyte** is the closer match to Electrolit than the classic bottle.

**The quick picks:**

- **Hangover where you were sick in the night, or a stomach bug:** Electrolit (or Gatorlyte if that's what's on the shelf).
- **Mild hangover, you feel thirsty but not sick:** either one, or just water and a salty breakfast. Pick what you'll actually drink.
- **Long run, game, or hard workout in the heat:** regular Gatorade, because you need the carbohydrate as fuel.
- **Watching sugar:** Gatorade Zero or a lower-sugar Electrolit version, and compare the labels.
- **A sick baby or young child:** neither, without checking with your pediatrician first. A pediatric oral rehydration solution is usually what they'll suggest.

> **When to see a doctor instead of reaching for a drink.** Electrolyte drinks are for mild dehydration. **Get medical care if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you haven't urinated in 8 hours or more, you feel faint or dizzy every time you stand, you're confused, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, or you have a high fever with severe diarrhea. **Call 911 right away** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no bottle of anything fixes that. If you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or see or hear things that aren't there within a day or two of stopping, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Tell a doctor or go to urgent care. If you have kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure, or take a medicine that raises potassium, ask your doctor before drinking electrolyte drinks regularly.

## Electrolit vs Gatorade: The Core Difference

The easiest way to understand these two drinks is to look at who they were made for.

**Gatorade** was created in the 1960s for University of Florida football players who were losing huge amounts of sweat in the Florida heat. Athletes in that situation lose water and some salt, but they also burn through carbohydrate. So the formula leans on sugar for energy and flavor, with a modest amount of sodium and potassium. It's now owned by PepsiCo and sold in almost every gas station, gym, and grocery store in the US.

**Electrolit** comes from a Mexican pharmaceutical company and has been sold in Mexico for years as a *suero oral*, an oral rehydration drink. In the last several years it has spread across US grocery stores, convenience stores, and big-box retailers, usually in a tall plastic bottle of about 21 fluid ounces (625 mL). It's designed for replacing lost fluid, not for fueling exercise.

That difference in purpose shows up in the label. Oral rehydration drinks are built around a specific idea from medical research: your small intestine absorbs water fastest when **sodium and glucose arrive together in the right ratio**. They share a transport system in the gut wall, and water follows them in. The World Health Organization's oral rehydration salts, used worldwide for diarrheal illness, are built on that principle. Electrolit is a consumer version of the same idea. Gatorade isn't, because it was never trying to be.

The practical result: **Electrolit has more salt and less sugar. Gatorade has less salt and more sugar.** Almost every other difference flows from that.

## Side-by-Side Comparison

Gatorade publishes consistent nutrition numbers across most flavors. Electrolit's numbers vary by flavor, by country of manufacture, and by version, and the formula has been adjusted over time. So for Electrolit, the honest advice is to **read the Nutrition Facts panel on the bottle in your hand**. The table below shows the general pattern, with Gatorade figures for its standard Thirst Quencher line.

| | Electrolit (regular) | Gatorade Thirst Quencher | Gatorlyte |
|---|---|---|---|
| Type of drink | Oral rehydration drink (*suero*) | Sports drink | Rapid-rehydration drink |
| Made by | Mexican pharmaceutical group | PepsiCo | PepsiCo |
| Typical bottle | About 21 fl oz (625 mL) | 12, 20, 28, or 32 fl oz | 20 fl oz |
| Sodium | Oral-rehydration range; well above Gatorade (check label) | About 160 mg per 12 fl oz | Much higher than regular Gatorade (check label) |
| Potassium | Yes; check label | About 50 mg per 12 fl oz | Much higher than regular Gatorade |
| Other minerals | Chloride, calcium, magnesium | Chloride | Chloride, calcium, magnesium |
| Sugar | Moderate glucose; check label | About 21 g per 12 fl oz | Much lower than regular Gatorade |
| Calories | Moderate | About 80 per 12 fl oz | Low |
| Sugar-free option | Lower-sugar versions in some markets | Gatorade Zero | No |
| Taste | Lightly sweet, slightly salty | Sweet, familiar | Saltier than regular Gatorade |
| Best for | Fluid loss from illness, hangover, heat | Long or intense exercise | Fluid loss when only Gatorade products are available |

Three things stand out.

1. **Sodium is the big gap.** Sodium is the electrolyte you lose most of through sweat, vomiting, and diarrhea, and it's the one that drives water absorption and helps you hold on to fluid. A standard Gatorade is light on it. Electrolit is built around it.
2. **Gatorade has a lot more sugar.** A 20-ounce bottle of regular Gatorade has roughly 34 grams of sugar, close to what you'd get from a can of soda. That's useful in the middle of a two-hour run. For someone lying on the couch with a queasy stomach, it's mostly extra sugar.
3. **Gatorlyte changes the picture.** Gatorade launched Gatorlyte because the classic formula is too light on electrolytes for serious fluid loss. Gatorlyte carries far more sodium and potassium than regular Gatorade and much less sugar, which puts it in the same neighborhood as Electrolit and Pedialyte. If you're comparing "Electrolit vs Gatorade" because you're standing in a store aisle, Gatorlyte is the fair comparison.

## Which Is Better for a Hangover?

For most hangovers, **Electrolit has the edge on paper, but the gap matters less than you'd think.** Here's why.

Alcohol does dehydrate you. It suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it around, you pee out more fluid than you take in. That's why you wake up thirsty, with a dry mouth and maybe a headache. Our explainer on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) covers the details.

But dehydration is only one piece of a hangover, and often not the biggest one. A widely cited review of hangover research in the *Annals of Internal Medicine* (Wiese and colleagues, 2000) noted that dehydration and blood electrolyte changes don't line up neatly with how bad people feel. Later reviews by hangover researchers have made the same point. The nausea, fatigue, foggy thinking, and that general poisoned feeling seem to come more from inflammation, broken sleep, stomach irritation, low blood sugar in some people, and acetaldehyde, the toxic chemical your body makes as it breaks alcohol down.

So there is no good evidence that Electrolit, Gatorade, or any electrolyte drink cures or prevents a hangover. What a good rehydration drink can do is:

- Replace fluid and salt faster than plain water, especially if you threw up or have diarrhea
- Ease thirst, dry mouth, and the lightheadedness that comes from being low on fluid
- Take the edge off the part of the headache that comes from dehydration
- Give you a little sugar if your blood sugar is low after drinking on an empty stomach

### When Electrolit clearly wins

If you were sick in the night or have diarrhea the next morning, you've lost real fluid and salt, and the stomach is irritated. That's exactly the situation oral rehydration drinks are designed for. Electrolit's higher sodium helps you absorb and hold on to the fluid, and its lower sugar is gentler on an upset gut. Large amounts of a sugary drink can pull water into the intestine and make diarrhea worse, which is one reason doctors steer people with stomach bugs away from regular sports drinks, juice, and soda as their main fluid.

### When it doesn't matter much

If you had a few drinks, slept badly, and wake up thirsty but not sick, the difference between Electrolit and Gatorade is small. Either one will help with the thirst. So will two big glasses of water and a breakfast with some salt in it, like eggs and toast or a bowl of soup. The best drink in this situation is the one you'll actually finish.

### Where Gatorade has a small advantage

Gatorade's extra sugar can help if you feel weak and shaky and haven't eaten. Alcohol can interfere with how your liver releases sugar into your blood, and some people wake up with the trembly, low-energy feeling that comes with low blood sugar. A few sips of something sweet can help. That said, eating actual food does the same job better and lasts longer. Our guide to [Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/gatorade-for-hangover) goes deeper on what regular Gatorade can and can't do.

## Electrolit vs Gatorlyte

This is the comparison people often mean without realizing it. Gatorlyte is Gatorade's answer to Pedialyte and Electrolit: a rapid-rehydration drink with a heavier electrolyte load, added magnesium and calcium, and far less sugar than the classic bottle.

On paper, Electrolit and Gatorlyte are close cousins. Both are built for replacing lost fluid rather than fueling a workout. The practical differences are:

- **Taste.** Gatorlyte tastes noticeably saltier than regular Gatorade. Many people find Electrolit's flavor milder and easier to sip when nauseated, but taste is personal.
- **Bottle size.** Electrolit's bottle is a little larger (about 21 fl oz vs 20 fl oz).
- **Sweeteners.** Check the ingredient list on both if you care about non-sugar sweeteners. Formulas and sweetener choices vary by product line and can change.
- **Availability.** Gatorlyte is easy to find anywhere Gatorade is sold. Electrolit is widely available now but may be missing from smaller stores.

If you're deciding between the two for a hangover or a stomach bug, either is a reasonable choice. Pick the one you like the taste of. We compare Gatorlyte against Pedialyte in more detail in our [Gatorlyte vs Pedialyte guide](/never-hungover/gatorlyte-vs-pedialyte).

## Electrolit vs Gatorade Zero

Gatorade Zero removes the sugar and keeps roughly the same sodium and potassium as regular Gatorade, using non-sugar sweeteners instead. It's a good choice if you like Gatorade's taste and want to avoid sugar, for example if you're managing diabetes or watching calories.

The trade-off is that oral rehydration works best with *some* glucose present, because sodium and glucose are absorbed together. A zero-sugar drink still hydrates you, and for a mild hangover that's fine. But for real fluid loss from vomiting or diarrhea, a drink built around the sodium-glucose balance, like Electrolit, Gatorlyte, or Pedialyte, is the better tool. Gatorade Zero's sodium is also still on the lighter side compared with an oral rehydration drink.

If you want a sugar-free option and plan to eat something with it, Gatorade Zero plus a salty snack is a perfectly sensible hangover morning. If you're too sick to eat, go with a proper rehydration drink.

## Electrolit vs Gatorade for Stomach Bugs, Vomiting, and Diarrhea

This is where the choice matters most, because dehydration from illness can become serious.

For **adults** with a stomach bug, Electrolit (or Gatorlyte, or Pedialyte) is the better choice than regular Gatorade. The reasons are the same as above: more sodium to replace what you're losing, and less sugar to avoid making diarrhea worse. Sip small amounts often, a few sips every few minutes, rather than drinking a lot at once. If you can't keep anything down, or you're getting dizzy, confused, or you've stopped urinating, get medical care rather than trying harder with the bottle.

If regular Gatorade is all you have, it's better than nothing for an adult with a mild bug. Some people dilute it with water to cut the sugar, but that also cuts the already-modest sodium, so pairing it with salty crackers or broth makes more sense.

For **babies and young children**, call your pediatrician. They'll usually recommend a pediatric oral rehydration solution with clear dosing directions by age and weight. Don't give a baby a sports drink, juice, or soda in place of a rehydration solution, and don't assume an adult-marketed drink is right for a small child without asking. Our [Electrolit vs Pedialyte comparison](/never-hungover/electrolit-vs-pedialyte) covers the pediatric side in more depth.

## Electrolit vs Gatorade for Exercise and Heat

Here the tables turn a bit.

For **long or intense exercise**, roughly an hour or more of hard effort, regular Gatorade does what it was designed to do. Your muscles are burning carbohydrate, and the sugar in Gatorade helps keep you going. Electrolit has less sugar, so it's less useful as fuel. Endurance athletes often use a sports drink during the workout and a higher-sodium drink, or salty food, afterward.

For **short workouts** under an hour, most people don't need either one. Water is fine.

For **working or spending a long day in the heat**, especially if you're sweating heavily and not eating much, a higher-sodium drink like Electrolit can make more sense than regular Gatorade, because sodium is the main thing you're losing in sweat. People who sweat a lot and drink only plain water for many hours can end up with low blood sodium, which is uncommon but can be dangerous. Mixing in salty food or an electrolyte drink helps prevent that.

For **heavy salty sweaters** (if your shirt dries with white salt marks), a higher-sodium option is worth considering for long efforts. Gatorade also sells higher-sodium lines aimed at endurance athletes, so check what's available.

## Sugar, Calories, and Sweeteners

Sugar is one of the biggest real differences between these drinks, so it's worth spelling out.

- **Regular Gatorade** is a sugary drink. A 20-ounce bottle has around 34 grams of sugar and 140 calories. If you drink a couple of bottles a day out of habit rather than because you're exercising, that adds up fast.
- **Electrolit** has a moderate amount of glucose, enough to support absorption but well below Gatorade. Exact amounts depend on the version and flavor.
- **Gatorade Zero** has no sugar and uses non-sugar sweeteners.
- **Gatorlyte** has much less sugar than regular Gatorade.

If you have **diabetes**, the sugar matters. A sugar-free option may suit you better day to day, but if you're sick and can't eat, ask your doctor or diabetes care team what they want you to drink, since many sick-day plans include some carbohydrate.

If you have **high blood pressure, kidney disease, or heart failure**, the sodium matters. Electrolit and Gatorlyte are higher in sodium than regular Gatorade. Occasional use is usually fine for healthy people, but if your doctor has told you to limit salt, check with them before making any electrolyte drink a regular habit.

## Taste, Price, and Where to Buy

**Taste.** This is personal, but there are some patterns. Regular Gatorade tastes sweet and familiar, which is a big part of why people reach for it. Electrolit tastes lighter and a little salty, and many people find it easier to drink than Pedialyte. Gatorlyte is saltier than regular Gatorade. When you're nauseated, a drink you can keep sipping beats a "better" drink you can't stand.

**Price.** Regular Gatorade is usually the cheapest per bottle, especially in multipacks or powder form. Electrolit and Gatorlyte typically cost more per bottle. Prices vary a lot by store and region, so compare per ounce rather than per bottle.

**Where to buy.** Gatorade is everywhere. Electrolit is now common in US grocery stores, pharmacies, convenience stores, and big-box retailers, and in neighborhoods with Mexican and Latin American grocers it's often stocked in the cooler. Gatorlyte is usually right next to the regular Gatorade.

**Cheaper alternatives.** If you want an oral rehydration drink without paying brand prices, store-brand oral rehydration solutions in the pharmacy aisle work on the same principle. You can also make a simple version at home; our [homemade electrolyte drink guide](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) walks through a safe recipe. Measure carefully, because too much salt or sugar defeats the purpose.

## Honest Pros and Cons

### Electrolit

**Pros**

- Built as an oral rehydration drink, with more sodium and less sugar than a sports drink
- Adds calcium and magnesium on top of sodium, potassium, and chloride
- Many people find it easier to drink than Pedialyte
- Larger bottle than most single-serve sports drinks
- A good match for hangovers with vomiting or diarrhea, and for stomach bugs in adults

**Cons**

- Usually more expensive per bottle than regular Gatorade
- Nutrition numbers vary by flavor and market, so you have to read the label
- Not as widely stocked as Gatorade in smaller stores
- Less useful as fuel during long, hard exercise
- Not a pediatric product; ask your pediatrician before giving it to a young child

### Gatorade

**Pros**

- Cheap and available almost everywhere
- Sugar provides real fuel for long or intense exercise
- Familiar taste that's easy to drink
- Gatorade Zero offers a sugar-free option, and Gatorlyte offers a true rehydration option within the same brand
- Fine for a mild hangover where you're just thirsty

**Cons**

- Regular Gatorade is high in sugar and relatively low in sodium for rehydration
- Not a good main fluid for diarrhea, since the sugar can make it worse
- Easy to drink a lot of sugar without noticing if you use it as an everyday drink
- Gatorade Zero has no glucose, so it's a weaker match for real fluid loss

## What About Pedialyte, Liquid IV, or Coconut Water?

These come up in the same conversation, so here's the short version.

- **Pedialyte** is the closest match to Electrolit: another oral rehydration solution, with a long track record in children. Many adults find it saltier and more medicinal tasting.
- **Liquid IV** is a powder you mix into water. It's built on the same sodium-glucose idea and is higher in sodium than regular Gatorade. Our [Liquid IV vs Gatorade comparison](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-vs-gatorade) has the details.
- **Coconut water** is naturally high in potassium but fairly low in sodium, so it's a weaker rehydration drink than its reputation suggests. It's fine as a light, pleasant drink, but not a substitute for an oral rehydration solution when you're sick.

For a broader look at all of these side by side, see our [electrolyte drinks for hangovers comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).

## How to Rehydrate the Morning After (Whichever Drink You Pick)

- **Start with what you have.** Water is the base. Add an electrolyte drink if you were sick, sweated a lot, or feel lightheaded.
- **Sip, don't chug.** A few sips every few minutes is easier on an upset stomach than half a bottle at once.
- **Drink it cold.** Both Electrolit and Gatorade taste better cold, and cold drinks are often easier to keep down.
- **Spread it out.** Your body can only absorb so much at a time. Aim to drink steadily over an hour or two rather than all at once.
- **Eat when you can.** Toast, crackers, rice, bananas, eggs, or a brothy soup give you carbohydrate and more salt. In Mexico, a bowl of *menudo* or *caldo* is a traditional cure for *la cruda*, and the salty broth does real rehydration work. Our guide to [traditional Mexican hangover remedies](/never-hungover/traditional-mexican-hangover-remedies-vs-modern-supplements) covers the classics.
- **One bottle is usually enough.** For a typical hangover in a healthy adult, one bottle of an electrolyte drink plus water and food for the rest of the day is plenty. More isn't better, and very large amounts add a lot of sodium or sugar.
- **Watch your urine.** Pale yellow means you're doing fine. Very dark urine or very little of it after several hours of drinking fluids is a reason to slow down and think about getting checked.

Our full guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) has more on timing and amounts.

## Should You Drink Electrolit or Gatorade Before Bed?

A lot of people try to head off a hangover by drinking an electrolyte drink before bed. It's not a bad habit, since going to sleep a little less dehydrated can mean a less parched morning. But there is no good evidence that drinking Electrolit or Gatorade before bed prevents a hangover. A big glass of water does much of the same job. If you do want something before bed, a lower-sugar option is kinder to your teeth and your sleep than a full-sugar sports drink.

What matters more happens during the night itself: eating before you drink, alternating alcoholic drinks with water, and drinking less overall. Our guide on [timing electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) looks at what the evidence does and doesn't support.

## A Better Plan Than Just Fixing the Morning

Electrolit and Gatorade both work on the symptoms after the fact. If you want to feel better the next day, the bigger levers are earlier in the night:

- **Eat a real meal before drinking.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
- **Alternate drinks with water.** One glass of water between alcoholic drinks cuts how much you drink and how dry you get.
- **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies from person to person.
- **Protect your sleep.** Poor sleep is one of the biggest drivers of how rough the next day feels.

Some people also add a supplement to their routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, is one of the more studied options. Animal research suggests it may affect how the body handles alcohol and its by-products, but human data is limited, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how people typically use it. Think of it as one small piece of the plan, not a replacement for water, food, and drinking less.

## The Bottom Line

Electrolit and regular Gatorade are different tools. Electrolit is an oral rehydration drink with more sodium and less sugar, which makes it the better choice for a hangover with vomiting or diarrhea, a stomach bug, or a long day sweating in the heat. Regular Gatorade is a sports drink whose extra sugar makes sense during long, hard exercise and not much else. If you're in a store with only Gatorade products, Gatorlyte is the closer match to Electrolit, and Gatorade Zero is the pick if you just want to avoid sugar. For a mild hangover, the difference is small, and water plus a salty breakfast does most of the work. And if you can't keep fluids down, haven't urinated in many hours, or someone can't be woken after drinking, skip the drink aisle and get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Electrolit better than Gatorade?**

For rehydration after vomiting, diarrhea, or a rough hangover, usually yes. Electrolit is an oral rehydration drink with more sodium and less sugar than regular Gatorade, which is the mix your gut absorbs best when you've lost fluid. For long or intense exercise, regular Gatorade's extra sugar gives you fuel that Electrolit doesn't. For a mild hangover where you're just thirsty, the difference is small.

**Which is better for a hangover, Electrolit or Gatorade?**

Electrolit has the edge, especially if you were sick in the night, because it replaces more sodium with less sugar. But dehydration is only one part of a hangover, so neither drink cures it. If all you have is Gatorade, it will still help with thirst and dry mouth, and Gatorlyte is a closer match to Electrolit than the classic bottle.

**What's the difference between Electrolit and Gatorlyte?**

They're similar. Both are rapid-rehydration drinks with more sodium and less sugar than regular Gatorade, and both add minerals like magnesium and calcium. The main differences are taste, bottle size, sweeteners, and price. Gatorlyte tastes saltier to many people, while Electrolit has a milder flavor. Either is a reasonable choice for a hangover or stomach bug.

**Does Electrolit have more sugar than Gatorade?**

No. Regular Electrolit has a moderate amount of glucose, well below regular Gatorade, which has roughly 34 grams of sugar in a 20-ounce bottle. Exact Electrolit amounts vary by flavor and market, so check the label. Gatorade Zero has no sugar at all.

**Is Electrolit good for a stomach bug?**

For adults with mild to moderate dehydration from a stomach bug, yes. It's an oral rehydration drink, so it's designed for this. Sip small amounts often. If you can't keep fluids down for several hours, stop urinating, or feel faint or confused, get medical care. For babies and young children, call your pediatrician first.

**Can I drink Electrolit every day?**

Healthy people can, but most don't need to. On a normal day, water and food give you the salt and fluid you need, and a daily bottle adds a fair amount of extra sodium and some sugar. If you have kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure, or take medicines that raise potassium, ask your doctor before drinking electrolyte drinks regularly.

**Is Gatorade Zero as good as Electrolit for rehydration?**

Not for real fluid loss. Gatorade Zero has no sugar and relatively modest sodium, while oral rehydration works best when sodium and a little glucose arrive together. Gatorade Zero is fine for a mild hangover, especially with a salty snack, but for vomiting or diarrhea, Electrolit, Gatorlyte, or Pedialyte is the better tool.

**Should I drink Electrolit or Gatorade before going to bed after drinking?**

A drink before bed can mean a slightly less parched morning, but there is no good evidence that it prevents a hangover. A big glass of water does much of the same job. Eating before you drink, alternating alcohol with water, and drinking less overall matter more than anything you drink at bedtime.
